newsitem.title: USA: U.S., S. Korea await North's answer on peace talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., S. Korea await North's answer on peace talks.

text.p: Crucial talks open on Wednesday on whether famine-threatened Stalinist North Korea is prepared to make a serious stab at peace with its prosperous democratic arch-rival in the south.

U.S. officials are cautiously optimistic Pyongyang would ultimately respond positively to Washington's year-old joint proposal with South Korea for four-party peace talks that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 Korean War.
But while they hope for a direct answer on Wednesday, U.S. negotiators are prepared for marathon discussions that may not produce a conclusive reply until perhaps on Friday.
"I think the North Koreans are congenitally unable to finish off a deal until they absolutely have rung every last bit of advantage out of it," a U.S. official told Reuters.

"That's understandable but they can't afford to walk away and we're probably going to spend hours on Wednesday convincing them that there is no further advantage to be gained (from withhold assent to the peace talks)," he said.
This may mean the meeting has to be carried over until Friday, but "once we have done that, I think they will give us an unequivocal yes," the official said in an interview.

It was expected North Korea might make a final pitch for massive additional food aid to compensate for two years of shortages due to flooding that the United States, as well as humanitarian groups, agree are devastating and worsening.
If Pyongyang agrees, the landmark peace negotiations, which would also include China, are not expected to begin until June or July due to preparations, including consultations with Beijing.

The talks aim to defuse tensions on the heavily-armed and volatile peninsula and resolve the 1950-53 Korean War that sealed the division between north and south by replacing the fraying armistice with a peace treaty.

On the eve of the crucial meeting with North Korea -- set for the U.N. PLaza Hotel in New York -- the United States on Tuesday announced $15 million in additional food aid to feed children in the famine-threatened Stalinist country.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the new donation, which brings total U.S. food aid to Pyongyang to $33.4 million since late 1995, was offered because the North's food shortages would reach a critical stage this spring.
The new aid comes on top of $10 million pledged in February that is due to arrive in North Korea in early May.
Burns said the offer was motivated by humanitarian concerns and was not linked with Wednesday's meeting of U.S., North Korean and South Korean officials in New York.
But U.S. officials have increasingly accepted that Pyongyang was unlikely to agree to peace talks until its dire food needs were met.

With the decision to provide an additional $15 million of aid in the form of 50,000 tonnes of U.S. corn, the United States would provide one quarter of the $95.5 million requested recently by U.N. World Food Programme.

The United States insists on funnelling all its food aid to North Korea via the WFP because it trusts that organisation to monitor the aid and ensure it goes to the intended recipients, in this case 2.4 million children under the age of six years.

North Korea agreed earlier this month to a barter with the huge grain dealer Cargill Inc, in which it would trade 4,000 tonnes of zinc for 20,000 tonnes of white wheat. U.S. officials and other experts say increased commercial deals are ultimately the only way Pyongyang can meet its urgent foods deals.

But Washington has backed limited deliveries of emergency food aid, believing it is in the U.S. interest not to let North Korea implode, unleashing instability, massive refugee flows and unpredictable reactions from the heavily-militarized regime.
